judge_reason: The assistant accurately identifies the factors for best execution and the definition of total consideration for retail clients, while also providing relevant context on how execution is monitored and demonstrated.
answer:
To achieve best execution, a firm must take all sufficient steps to obtain the best possible result for its clients by considering several key factors [MiFID II | Article 27 (Obligation to execute orders on terms most favourable to the client), p. 64].

### Factors to Consider
When executing orders, firms must consider the following factors:
*   **Primary factors:** Price, costs, speed, likelihood of execution and settlement, size, nature, or any other consideration relevant to the execution of the order [MiFID II | Article 27 (Obligation to execute orders on terms most favourable to the client), p. 64].
*   **Relative importance:** The importance of these factors is determined by the characteristics of the client (e.g., retail vs. professional), the order itself, the financial instrument, and the available execution venues [MiFID II Delegated Regulation | Article 64 (Best execution criteria), pp. 57-58].
*   **Specific Instructions:** If a client provides a specific instruction, the firm must follow it [MiFID II | Article 27 (Obligation to execute orders on terms most favourable to the client), p. 64]. A clear and prominent warning must be provided that such instructions may prevent the firm from taking the steps designed to obtain the best possible result [MiFID II Delegated Regulation | Article 66 (Execution policy), pp. 59-60].

### Measurement for Retail Clients
For retail clients, the "best possible result" is determined in terms of **total consideration** [MiFID II | Article 27 (Obligation to execute orders on terms most favourable to the client), p. 64]. This represents:
*   The price of the financial instrument.
*   The costs relating to execution, including all expenses incurred by the client that are directly related to the execution, such as execution venue fees, clearing and settlement fees, and any other fees paid to third parties [MiFID II | Article 27 (Obligation to execute orders on terms most favourable to the client), p. 64].

Firms monitor and demonstrate the quality of execution through several mechanisms:
*   **Monitoring and Review:** Firms must monitor the effectiveness of their execution arrangements and policy, assessing on a regular basis whether the chosen execution venues provide the best possible result [MiFID II | Article 27 (Obligation to execute orders on terms most favourable to the client), p. 65].
*   **Public Reporting:** Execution venues must publish data on the quality of execution (price, costs, speed, and likelihood of execution) annually [MiFID II | Article 27 (Obligation to execute orders on terms most favourable to the client), p. 65]. Additionally, firms must summarize and publish their top five execution venues by trading volume and provide information on the quality of execution obtained [MiFID II | Article 27 (Obligation to execute orders on terms most favourable to the client), p. 65].
*   **Demonstration:** Firms must be able to demonstrate to clients, upon request, that orders were executed in accordance with the firm's execution policy [MiFID II | Article 27 (Obligation to execute orders on terms most favourable to the client), p. 65].

This notification must be provided no later than the end of the business day in which the threshold is exceeded, or by the close of the next business day if the threshold is exceeded on a non-business day [MiFID II Delegated Regulation | Article 62 (Additional reporting obligations for portfolio management or contingent liability transactions), p. 56]. Investment firms that hold client financial instruments or client funds shall send a statement of those assets to each client at least on a quarterly basis [MiFID II Delegated Regulation | Article 63 (Statements of client financial instruments or client funds), pp. 56-57].

This requirement is subject to the following:
*   The statement is not required if it has been provided in any other periodic statement [MiFID II Delegated Regulation | Article 63 (Statements of client financial instruments or client funds), pp. 56-57].
*   Firms shall provide the statement more frequently upon client request at a commercial cost [MiFID II Delegated Regulation | Article 63 (Statements of client financial instruments or client funds), pp. 56-57].
*   The statement does not need to be provided if the firm provides the client with access to an online system (qualifying as a durable medium) where up-to-date statements can be easily accessed and the firm has evidence that the client has accessed the statement at least once during the relevant quarter [MiFID II Delegated Regulation | Article 63 (Statements of client financial instruments or client funds), p. 57].

*   **Collect information:** The firm must collect the necessary information on the client's existing investments and the recommended new investments [MiFID II Delegated Regulation | Article 54 (Assessment of suitability and suitability reports), pp. 51-52].
*   **Analyze costs and benefits:** The firm must undertake an analysis of the costs and benefits of the switch [MiFID II Delegated Regulation | Article 54 (Assessment of suitability and suitability reports), pp. 51-52].

A professional client is defined as a client who possesses the experience, knowledge, and expertise to make their own investment decisions and properly assess the risks they incur [MiFID II | ANNEX II (PROFESSIONAL CLIENTS FOR THE PURPOSE OF THIS DIRECTIVE), p. 135].

While investment firms are required to provide professional clients with information on the nature of financial instruments and their associated risks, the level of detail may vary compared to that provided to retail clients [MiFID II Delegated Regulation | Recitals, p. 9]. Firms must provide this information in good time before the provision of services, ensuring it is sufficient to enable the client to make informed investment decisions [MiFID II Delegated Regulation | Article 48 (Information about financial instruments), pp. 45-46].

If a client is being treated as a professional upon request (rather than being automatically classified as one), the firm must perform an adequate assessment of the client's expertise, experience, and knowledge to gain reasonable assurance that the client is capable of understanding the risks involved [MiFID II | ANNEX II (PROFESSIONAL CLIENTS FOR THE PURPOSE OF THIS DIRECTIVE), p. 136]. It remains the responsibility of a professional client to request a higher level of protection if they deem themselves unable to properly assess or manage the risks involved [MiFID II | ANNEX II (PROFESSIONAL CLIENTS FOR THE PURPOSE OF THIS DIRECTIVE), p. 136].

answer:
Yes, a national competent authority may prohibit or restrict the marketing, distribution, or sale of structured deposits in or from its Member State [MiFIR | Article 42 (Product intervention by competent authorities), pp. 53-54].

This action can be taken if the authority is satisfied on reasonable grounds that [MiFIR | Article 42 (Product intervention by competent authorities), pp. 53-54]:
*   The structured deposit or activity gives rise to significant investor protection concerns, poses a threat to the orderly functioning and integrity of financial markets, or threatens the stability of the financial system [MiFIR | Article 42 (Product intervention by competent authorities), pp. 53-54].
*   Existing regulatory requirements do not sufficiently address these risks [MiFIR | Article 42 (Product intervention by competent authorities), pp. 53-54].
*   The action is proportionate [MiFIR | Article 42 (Product intervention by competent authorities), pp. 53-54].
*   The authority has properly consulted other affected competent authorities [MiFIR | Article 42 (Product intervention by competent authorities), pp. 53-54].
*   The action is not discriminatory [MiFIR | Article 42 (Product intervention by competent authorities), pp. 53-54].

The authority may impose such a prohibition or restriction on a precautionary basis before the product has been marketed, distributed, or sold [MiFIR | Article 42 (Product intervention by competent authorities), p. 54]. Generally, the authority must notify other competent authorities and ESMA at least one month before the measure takes effect, though urgent action can be taken on a provisional basis in exceptional cases [MiFIR | Article 42 (Product intervention by competent authorities), p. 54].

If a firm does not obtain this information, it must not recommend investment services or financial instruments to the client [MiFID II Delegated Regulation | Article 54 (Assessment of suitability and suitability reports), p. 51].

Regarding recommendations, the firm must ensure that the recommended investment services and financial instruments are suitable for the client, particularly in accordance with their risk tolerance and ability to bear losses [MiFID II | Article 25 (Assessment of suitability and appropriateness and reporting to clients), pp. 60-61]. *   Up to EUR 700,000; or
*   Up to twice the amount of the profits gained or losses avoided because of the infringement, where those can be determined [PRIIPs | Article 24, pp. 19-20].

Member States may decide not to lay down rules for administrative sanctions for infringements that are already subject to criminal sanctions under their national law [PRIIPs | Article 22, p. 19].
